Brat
BRAT
adjective / noun (Gen-Z slang)
From English brat, a contemptuous word for a child (1500s). In June 2024 British singer Charli XCX released the album Brat, with a plain lime-green cover, and described a brat as a girl who is a little messy, likes to party, sometimes says dumb things, and is confident about it anyway. "Brat summer" became the season’s meme, spread into fashion, advertising, and even politics, and Collins Dictionary named brat its Word of the Year for 2024.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang to be brat is to have a defiant, messy, unapologetic confidence: the girl who parties, says what she wants, makes a mess, and refuses to be sorry. "Brat summer" meant a season of living that way, and the lime-green aesthetic was everywhere. The Christian observation: the word was well chosen, because its old meaning has not gone away. A brat is a child who has never been told no, and Scripture is clear about where that leads: "Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him" (Pro 22:15), and "a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame" (Pro 29:15). The trend takes the untrained child and calls her an icon. Paul lists the marks of the last days, and a brat summer could be the summary: "lovers of their own selves... disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy" (2Ti 3:2). The confidence Scripture commends is a different thing — "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4) — and it is not timid; meekness is strength under God’s rule. "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right" (Eph 6:1). A father tells his daughter: you do not need to be messy to be free, or loud to be confident; the most self-possessed woman in the room is the one who belongs to Christ and has nothing to prove.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (Charli XCX’s album Brat, June 2024; "brat summer"; Collins Word of the Year 2024) for a defiant, messy, unapologetic confidence — the old spoiled child rebranded as an icon, which Scripture answers with correction and a meek and quiet spirit (1Pe 3:4).

expand to see more

BRAT, adj. and n. (Gen-Z slang, 2024–present; from Charli XCX’s album Brat) Having a defiant, messy, party-loving, unapologetic confidence; a person or style with that attitude. "She showed up to the dance in lime green. So brat."

Brat summer: a season of carefree, pleasure-seeking, messy living (2024). Brat green: the album’s lime colour.

Older sense a grandparent knows: a spoiled, ill-behaved child ("a spoiled brat"); military brat, a child raised on bases (affectionate).

Webster (1828), root word brat: “BRAT, noun A child, so called in contempt. 1. Offspring; progeny.”

Decode for parents: an aesthetic of partying and defiance sold to girls as confidence. Show your daughter a better kind.

Key Scripture

Pro 22:15 — "Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him."

Pro 29:15 — "The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame."

2Ti 3:2 — "For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Eph 6:1 — "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right."

Modern Corruption

Brat rebrands the spoiled, untrained child as a model of female confidence; Scripture names the folly bound in a child’s heart and offers a meek and quiet spirit as the real strength.

expand to see more

The marketing was clever. Take a word every grandmother uses for a child who screams in the grocery store, attach it to a party album and a colour, and sell it back to young women as freedom. The brat is messy, impulsive, self-centred, and proud of it. Scripture describes that child exactly and does not admire her: "a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame" (Pro 29:15). Folly is not a personality; it is the natural state of an untrained heart, and love works to drive it out (Pro 22:15).

The trend also confuses confidence with defiance. A girl who answers back, breaks rules, and never apologizes looks strong for a summer; by thirty she is often lonely and tired. Paul’s catalogue of the last days — "lovers of their own selves... disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy" (2Ti 3:2) — reads like a mood board for it. Peter offers the alternative, and it is not weakness: a hidden beauty, "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4), calm because it is secure in God. Teach your daughters that the freest woman is the one who obeys God gladly and owes the crowd nothing.
